imageInfo.caption: No likeness of Muhammad al-Nasir survives; this is Bab Mahrouk, the gate of Fez he built in 1204 when he rebuilt the city walls, photographed in 1913.
imageInfo.creator: Stéphane Passet, autochrome for the Archives de la Planète
imageInfo.note: Commons and Wikipedia were searched for manuscript images, seals, portrait coins and later artwork of al-Nasir. None exists: his dinars bear only inscriptions, and Van Halen's 1864 Las Navas de Tolosa shows no figure identifiable as him. The Las Huelgas banner in Burgos is an artefact, not a monument. Bab Mahrouk was built in 1204 under al-Nasir as part of his rebuilding of the walls of Fez (Métalsi 2003; Archnet).

overview: Muhammad al-Nasir was Almohad caliph and commander defeated by the Iberian Christian coalition at Las Navas de Tolosa.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Muhammad al-Nasir was Almohad caliph and commander defeated by the Iberian Christian coalition at Las Navas de Tolosa. His reign shows the strain on Almohad power after the high point of the twelfth century, when North African imperial rule had to defend al-Andalus against increasingly coordinated Christian kingdoms.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Muhammad al-Nasir was born unknown, associated with Almohad Caliphate. The early evidence is uneven, so precise details should be treated carefully.
His background belonged to the world of Almohad Caliphate, where dynastic claims, military service, and aristocratic alliances shaped political careers.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Muhammad al-Nasir, the Almohad caliph, is remembered chiefly through the catastrophic defeat at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, and his character survives mostly in the shadow of that disaster. The sources — both the triumphant Christian accounts and the more critical Muslim ones — present a ruler whose reign marked the turning point of Almohad decline, and who failed to retrieve a battle that broke his army.

Arabic tradition tended to judge him harshly in hindsight, contrasting the scale of the defeat with the resources he commanded and questioning his leadership in the field. Christian sources, naturally, magnified the providential nature of their victory over him. Between these partisan extremes, the individual man is hard to recover.

What the record supports is a caliph who presided over a decisive reversal in Almohad fortunes and could not master the crisis it created, dying not long after. He is remembered as the defeated commander of Las Navas — a ruler associated with the collapse of Almohad power in Iberia rather than with any clearly drawn personal qualities.

contentSections.title: As Almohad caliph
paragraphs: He inherited a large Almohad realm spanning North Africa and al-Andalus. His Iberian campaign was meant to maintain Almohad pressure but ended in a damaging defeat.
Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa gives Muhammad al-Nasir's career a specific military and political setting: his choices, command, defeat, or death affected the outcome remembered in that article.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died at Marrakesh in 1213 after the Almohad defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa damaged his authority.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: His reign is remembered through the turning point of 1212, though Almohad decline had wider political and regional causes.
